treatments.summary: Gentle removal of impacted wax, debris or discharge using a fine suction tip under an operating microscope. No water, no syringing and no anaesthetic.
who: Blocked or muffled ear from impacted wax
Wax that did not clear with drops, or a history of eardrum perforation
Ear canal debris or discharge from an outer-ear infection (otitis externa)
Hearing aid users who need regular canal cleaning

steps.d: We ask about pain, discharge, past ear surgery and any eardrum hole, then look in with an otoscope.
Very hard wax may need olive-oil or sodium-bicarbonate drops for 3–5 days before the visit.
You lie on the couch while the doctor removes the wax under the microscope. You will hear a loud hissing sound, but it should not hurt.
We examine the cleaned canal and eardrum, and book a hearing test if your hearing still feels reduced.

recovery.d: Most people notice the change at once
Brief light-headedness can occur and settles

risks: Brief dizziness or a loud noise sensation during suction
Minor scratch or small bleed from the canal skin
Rarely, temporary ringing (tinnitus) after the clean
Eardrum injury is very rare under direct microscope view

faq.q: Is microsuction better than ear syringing?
faq.a: It is safer for most people. The doctor sees the canal throughout, so there is no water pressure on the eardrum and it can be used even if you have a perforation.
It is usually painless. Some people find the noise loud or feel a cool draught; we pause whenever you ask.

faq.q: Should I use cotton buds afterwards?
faq.a: No. Buds push wax deeper and can scratch the canal. Clean only the outer ear with a towel.
Yes, if they can sit or lie still. Our paediatric ENT team sees younger children with a parent present.

steps.d: CT of the temporal bone, hearing tests and an anaesthesia check, usually over two visits.
Through a cut behind the ear, disease is removed from the middle ear and mastoid bone, and the eardrum is rebuilt with a graft.

treatments.name: Grommet insertion
treatments.helps: Fluid behind the eardrum, mostly in children
treatments.summary: Tiny ventilation tubes placed in the eardrum to drain sticky fluid (glue ear) and restore hearing. Children usually go home within a few hours.
who: Glue ear in both ears lasting more than 3 months with hearing loss
Speech delay or school difficulties linked to poor hearing
Repeated middle-ear infections, several a year
Adults with persistent fluid after a cold or flight

steps.d: Hearing test and tympanometry confirm fluid. We often wait and watch for 3 months first.
Under a short anaesthetic, a tiny cut is made in the eardrum, the fluid is suctioned and a grommet is placed.
Children wake within minutes and usually go home after a drink and a snack.
Ear check and hearing test at 6 weeks, then every 6 months until the grommets fall out.

recovery.d: Mild ear ache settles with paracetamol

risks: Some discharge from the ear, treated with drops
Grommets may fall out early or, rarely, stay too long and need removal
A small hole may remain in the eardrum (about 1–2%)
Fluid can return after the grommets come out

faq.q: Can my child swim with grommets?
faq.a: Surface swimming is usually fine after 2 weeks. Avoid diving and dirty water; we may suggest earplugs for bath time.

faq.q: Do grommets need to be removed?
faq.a: Usually not. They fall out on their own in 6–12 months as the eardrum grows.

faq.q: Will adenoids be removed at the same time?
faq.a: Sometimes. If large adenoids are causing the fluid, removing them can lower the chance of glue ear returning.
Most children have little or no pain afterwards. Paracetamol for a day is usually enough.

A careful look and feel of the lips, gums, tongue, cheeks and palate.

treatments.helps: Overnight test in your own bed
treatments.summary: A small, easy-to-wear kit that records breathing, oxygen and snoring overnight in your own bed, to diagnose obstructive sleep apnoea without a hospital stay.
who: Loud snoring with pauses in breathing noticed by a partner
Daytime sleepiness, morning headaches or poor concentration
High blood pressure, diabetes or obesity with snoring
Before snoring or airway surgery, to measure severity

steps.d: Sleep questionnaire, nose and throat examination and a check of your BMI and neck size.
Our technician shows you how to wear the chest belt, nasal sensor and finger probe.
Sleep as usual. The kit records automatically and you return it the next morning.
A sleep physician scores the study and you get a report with the AHI and a treatment plan.

risks: No medical risk
Sensors may slip off; the test is repeated free if data is incomplete
Home studies can underestimate mild apnoea; a lab study may be advised
Not suitable for some heart or lung conditions

faq.q: Is a home study as good as a lab study?
faq.a: For most adults with suspected moderate to severe sleep apnoea, yes. It is more comfortable and you sleep more naturally.

faq.q: Can I take my usual medicines?
faq.a: Yes, take your normal medicines. Avoid alcohol and sleeping pills that night.
The apnoea-hypopnoea index counts breathing pauses per hour. Under 5 is normal; 30 or more is severe.

faq.q: What if I have sleep apnoea?
faq.a: Options include CPAP, weight loss, positional therapy, oral devices and, in selected cases, surgery.

Large tonsils with sleep apnoea in adults

steps.d: Sleep study, DISE and examination decide which levels need surgery.
Expansion sphincter pharyngoplasty, tonsillectomy, nasal surgery or tongue-base reduction as planned.
You stay one night with oxygen monitoring and pain control.
Review at 2 weeks and a repeat sleep study at 3 months.

risks: Sore throat for 10–14 days and bleeding risk similar to tonsillectomy

faq.q: Will surgery cure my sleep apnoea?
faq.a: It can greatly reduce it, especially when the collapse is at one level. A repeat sleep study at 3 months measures the result.
CPAP is the most effective treatment if you can use it. Surgery is for people who cannot, or as a way to make CPAP easier.
Weight loss helps a lot and we encourage it alongside any treatment.

faq.q: Is snoring surgery covered by insurance?
faq.a: Surgery for proven sleep apnoea is usually covered. Surgery only for snoring often is not.
